issues.legal_issue: Suo motu revisional power without a prescribed limitation period must be exercised within a reasonable time, including when the proposed correction is based on alleged fraud.
material_facts: The revenue entries showing the predecessors of the landholders were made in the mid-1950s and remained unchallenged for decades.
The landholders’ predecessors were recorded in the revenue records, the landholders purchased the land under registered deeds, and land revenue was continuously paid.
The government allotted land in the same survey areas for housing in 1991 without then taking action to correct the entries.
The government issued the challenged revision notice in 2004, seeking correction of entries made about fifty years earlier.
A civil court decree concerning plots in the survey area had become final, and the notice gave no explanation for the delay.
issues.conclusion: The proposed revision was exercised after an unreasonable delay and was arbitrary; the notice was rightly quashed.
issues.legal_principle: Even when a statute or regulation prescribes no limitation period, revisional power must be exercised within a reasonable time. What is reasonable depends on the circumstances, including the nature of the power, the delay, the affected rights and any explanation. Alleging fraud does not permit correction indefinitely; where fraud is relied on, power must be exercised within a reasonable time from its discovery. The Court applied Section 166B of the Andhra Pradesh (Telangana Area) Land Revenue Act, 1317F and relied on Collector v. P. Mangamma, State of Maharashtra v. Rattanlal, State of Orissa v. Brundaban Sharma, State of Gujarat v. Patil Raghav Natha, Mohamad Kavi Mohamad Amin v. Fatmabai Ibrahim, Santoshkumar Shivgonda Patil v. Balasaheb Tukaram Shevale, State of Punjab v. Bhatinda District Cooperative Milk Producers Union Ltd., Ibrahimpatnam Taluk Vyavasaya Coolie Sangham v. K. Suresh Reddy, S.B. Gurbaksh Singh v. Union of India, Sulochana Chandrakant Galande v. Pune Municipal Transport, State of H.P. v. Rajkumar Brijender Singh, and M/s Dehri Rohtas Light Railway Company Ltd. v. District Board, Bhojpur. The Court also noted that entries in the relevant record of rights were presumed true until the contrary was proved under Regulation 13 of the Andhra Pradesh (Telangana Area) Record of Rights in Land Regulation, 1358F.

rule.if: suo_motu_revision_to_correct_revenue_entries and no_fixed_limitation_period and entries_remained_unchallenged_for_decades and authority_had_prior_opportunity_to_review_entries and affected_parties_acquired_settled_interests and no_cogent_delay_explanation

predicates.suo_motu_revision_to_correct_revenue_ent: An authority initiated revision on its own initiative to correct entries in official land records.
predicates.no_fixed_limitation_period: The governing scheme set no fixed limitation period for the authority to exercise the revision power.
predicates.entries_remained_unchallenged_for_decade: The entries targeted for correction remained unchallenged for several decades.
predicates.authority_had_prior_opportunity_to_revie: The authority had an earlier occasion to review the relevant records but did not then challenge the entries.
predicates.affected_parties_acquired_settled_intere: People affected by the proposed correction had acquired interests and relied on the land records over time.
predicates.no_cogent_delay_explanation: The authority did not provide a cogent explanation for the delay in initiating revision.

issues.definition: When an authority initiates revision to correct long-standing land-record entries without a fixed time limit, its action is invalid as unreasonably delayed if it had an earlier opportunity to review the entries, affected people acquired settled interests, and no cogent explanation accounts for the delay.

issues.legal_issue: A revision notice relying on alleged fraud must state when the fraud was discovered when that discovery is relied on to justify the timing of the revisional action.
material_facts: The notice described the land-record entries as fraudulent but did not state when the alleged fraud had been discovered.
The government had allotted land in the same survey area for housing in 1991 and was presumed to have known the relevant revenue records then.
The notice was issued in 2004, and the government offered no explanation even for the delay measured from the 1991 allotment.
issues.conclusion: The notice did not assert an essential jurisdictional fact concerning discovery of the alleged fraud, and the attempt to justify the notice as timely from discovery was futile.
issues.legal_principle: Where revisional power based on fraud is said to run from discovery, it must be exercised within a reasonable time from discovery, and the date or period of discovery is a jurisdictional fact that must be clearly asserted in the notice. Merely describing an entry as fraudulent does not extend the power indefinitely. The Court applied Section 166B of the Andhra Pradesh (Telangana Area) Land Revenue Act, 1317F and relied particularly on Ibrahimpatnam Taluk Vyavasaya Coolie Sangham v. K. Suresh Reddy, as well as the reasonable-time principles stated in S.B. Gurbaksh Singh v. Union of India and the other authorities cited in the judgment.

predicates.suo_motu_revision_notice_alleges_fraud: An authority issued a notice in a proceeding initiated on its own initiative to revise an earlier decision or record, and the notice alleges fraud.
predicates.authority_relies_on_discovery_to_justify: The authority relies on the time of discovery of the alleged fraud to justify when it initiated the proceeding.
predicates.notice_omits_when_fraud_was_discovered: The notice does not clearly state when the alleged fraud was discovered.

issues.definition: A notice in a suo motu revision alleging fraud is invalid for omitting a jurisdictional fact when the authority relies on discovery to justify the timing but the notice does not say when discovery occurred.
